title: Efficacy comparison of intensive acute phoniatric intervention (IPA), voice therapy and psychotherapy for dissociative voice disorder (aphonia and dysphonia)
summary:
In this study, we want to scientifically test the effectiveness of different treatment methods for dissociative voice disorders. “Dissociative” means that the cause of the voice disorder is an altered connection between certain parts of the brain. This means that normal functions such as movement and voice can suddenly no longer work properly, even though no physical cause can be found. Voice loss is divided into dysphonia and aphonia. Dysphonia is a partial loss of voice, where the voice sounds hoarse, raspy or weak. With aphonia, the voice is completely lost. 
Our aim is to compare the effectiveness of the previously established therapy with a new therapy. The previously established therapy is a combination of speech therapy and psychotherapy. The new therapy is intensive phoniatric acute intervention (IPA). We want to find out whether IPA is just as effective or more effective than standard psychotherapy. IPA comprises one to a maximum of two intensive 1 to 3-hour therapy sessions. Standard psychotherapy consists of 12 sessions, which take place once a week.
We also want to check whether dissociative voice disorders are associated with changes in the brain and whether these are influenced by the two therapy approaches. For this reason, we take MRI images of the head at the beginning and end of the study. 
In summary, this will lead to a better understanding of the disorder in the long term and thus also to an improved therapeutic approach to dissociative voice disorders.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All participants:
- are between 18 and 69 years old
- use German as their first or main language
- have right-handedness

Patients with dissociative voice disorders:
- have a diagnosed dissociative voice disorder (psychogenic dysphonia/aphonia)
- have already received speech therapy treatment of at least 10 therapy hours
Exclusion criteria:
All participants:
- left-handedness, ambidexterity (using the Edinburgh handedness questionnaire (EHI))
- motor, cognitive, anatomical or sensory disorders that may be associated with speech and voice deficits
- speech fluency disorder (stuttering, poluttering)
- profound developmental disorder (e.g. autism) and severe congenital somatic diseases
- pre-existing severe concomitant mental illness (schizophrenia, history of psychotic episode, severe depressive episode, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, personality disorder according to DSM-V, current or history of substance-related addiction) 
- severe cognitive disorder (delirium, dementia) 
- central nervous system medication taken within the last 3 months
- acute influence of psychoactive substances (alcohol, cannabis, etc.) at the time of the study
- MRI contraindications (e.g. metallic objects in/on the body, pregnancy, breastfeeding, claustrophobia)

Patients with dissociative voice disorders:
- existence of dysphonia / aphonia for more than 2 years
- ongoing speech therapy
- previous psychotherapy within the last 5 years or > 30 hours of psychotherapy
